label: Clear_Cell_RCC
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Most common adult renal carcinoma subtype (~65–70% of RCC cases)
- Typically arises in renal cortex; peak incidence ages 60–70, M:F ~2:1
- Classic histology: nests/alveoli of clear cells with chicken-wire capillaries
- Strong, box-like membranous CA9/CAIX and PAX8; usually negative/focal CK7
- Inactivation of VHL (3p25) in up to 60% of cases
- Staged by AJCC 8th edition; prognosis worsens with grade, stage, necrosis, sarcomatoid features

## Terminology

- Definition: Malignant epithelial tumor of renal tubular origin, composed predominantly of clear cells with characteristic capillary network
- Synonyms (not recommended/outdated): hypernephroma, Grawitz tumor, nephrocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type)  
  - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**
  - Tumor composed of nests, alveoli, or sheets of malignant epithelial cells with clear cytoplasm (glycogen/lipid-rich)
  - Delicate, branching ("chicken-wire") capillary vascular network
  - Immunoprofile: strong and diffuse membranous CA9/CAIX ("box-like"), PAX8 positive, RCC marker, CD10 positive; usually negative CK7 or only focally positive  
    - [Gu Practical, p.826](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=826)
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/stainsrcc.html)
  - Absence of extensive papillary, chromophobe, or MiT-family features
- **Desirable:**
  - Identification of VHL gene mutation or promoter hypermethylation (up to 60%)  
    - [Gu Practical, p.826](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=826)
  - Confirmatory imaging of renal mass and exclusion of metastasis

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- Cell of origin: renal proximal tubular epithelium
- Molecular:
  - Loss of function (mutation, deletion, or hypermethylation) of VHL gene (3p25) in ~60% of cases
  - Sporadic: associated with risk factors (obesity, smoking, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, industrial chemical exposure)
  - Hereditary: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome—germline VHL mutation; multifocal/bilateral tumors in ~50% VHL cases
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)
- Potential precursor lesion: microscopic clear cell changes in renal parenchyma  
  - [Gu Practical, p.684](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=684)

## Clinical Issues

- **Epidemiology:**
  - ~65–70% of all adult RCC; peak age 60–70; M:F ~2:1
  - Estimated 81,800 new US cases/year (2023 data)
  - Highest incidences in Belarus, Eastern Europe, US  
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)
- **Presentation:**
  - Common: asymptomatic/incidental on imaging (37–61%)
  - Classic triad (10%): hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass
  - Large tumors at diagnosis historically
  - Paraneoplastic syndromes in ~20% (e.g., hypercalcemia, polycythemia, amyloidosis)
- **Site:**
  - Kidney—usually renal cortex; rare extrarenal RCC exist
- **Prognosis:**
  - 5-year survival ~70% overall, but highly dependent on stage (94% stage I; 80% stage II; 60% stage III; 5–10% stage IV)  
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)
- **Treatment:**
  - Localized: surgical resection (partial or radical nephrectomy)
  - Metastatic: immune checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase/anti-VEGF agents (for clear cell but less so for others)
  - Active surveillance in select low-risk patients

## Staging

- AJCC 8th edition TNM system is used
  - pT1a: ≤4 cm, limited to kidney
  - pT1b: >4–7 cm, limited to kidney
  - pT2a: >7–10 cm, limited to kidney
  - pT2b: >10 cm, limited to kidney
  - pT3a: extension into renal vein, perirenal fat, renal sinus fat/pelvicalyceal system
  - pT3b: extends into vena cava below diaphragm
  - pT4: beyond Gerota's fascia, direct adrenal invasion  
    - [Pathology Outlines Staging](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantstaging.html)
    - Measurement excludes extension into vein/IVC

## Macroscopic

- Typically unilateral, unifocal mass—but can be multifocal/bilateral (esp. in VHL)
- Bright yellow/orange (high lipid), well circumscribed, often with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis
- Cut surface may show solid, cystic, and hemorrhagic regions
  - Tumors with sarcomatoid change may be large (>10 cm), white/fleshy, heterogeneous  
    - ![Gross features—sarcomatoid clear cell RCC](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/_asset_library/textbooks/Gu_Practical/page_images/Gu_Practical_page_0861.png)  
      [Gu Practical, p.861](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=861)
  - Diffusely infiltrative variants exist

## Microscopic

- Nests/alveoli/sheets of clear cells with optically clear cytoplasm (glycogen/lipid-rich)
- Delicate, fine branching (“chicken-wire”) capillary vascular network surrounds nests
- Capillaries can impart a “nested-alveolar” or trabecular appearance
- Nuclei: round/oval, central or slightly eccentric; nucleoli grade varies (see grading)
- May show cystic change, hemorrhage, necrosis, variable architectural patterns (papillary, tubular, solid areas)
- High grade: pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, multinucleated giant cells, sarcomatoid/rhabdoid features
- Rare rhabdoid/sarcomatoid dedifferentiation (poor prognosis)
- In VHL syndrome: sometimes more papillary/tubulopapillary, but IHC/molecular profile is classic
- Peritumoral “clear cell changes” in cortex may be seen
- Precursor: microscopic foci (<1 mm) of clear cells in cortex can be considered possible precursors  
  - [Gu Practical, p.684](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=684)
- Figures:  
  ![Classic microscopic features: nests of clear cells, chicken-wire capillaries](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/kidneytumormalignantrcc01Tretiakova.jpeg)  
  ![Alveolar/nested pattern, clear cytoplasm](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-public-figures-830130787988/textbook_figures_web_v1/gu_practical/gu_practical_p0687_fig01_figure_33_24.jpeg)  
  ![Large nests with clear cytoplasm, capillary network](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/_asset_library/textbooks/Gu_Practical/page_images/Gu_Practical_page_0926.png)

## Ancillary Tests

- **Immunohistochemistry:**
  - CA9/CAIX: diffuse, box-like membranous positivity (hallmark)
  - PAX8: positive
  - RCC marker (renal cell carcinoma antigen): positive, but less sensitive/specific than PAX8, CA9
  - CD10: positive
  - Vimentin: positive
  - EMA: positive
  - CK7: negative or only focally positive (<25% of cases)
  - AMACR: negative (may be weakly positive in granular cell components)
  - AE1/AE3: may be focally positive
  - [Gu Practical, p.826](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=826)
  - [Pathology Outlines RCC IHC](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/stainsrcc.html)
  - ![IHC of clear cell renal tumors](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/kidneytumormalignantrccShah02.jpg)

- **Molecular:**
  - VHL gene mutation, deletion, or promoter hypermethylation in up to 60%
  - Loss of chromosome 3p (frequent, as VHL is at 3p25)  
    - [Gu Practical, p.826](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=826)
- **Electron Microscopy:**
  - Abundant cytoplasmic lipid and glycogen
  - Numerous mitochondria

## Radiology

- **Ultrasound:** RCC may be solid or cystic; can be hyper, iso, or hypoechoic
- **CT:** Modality of choice; clear cell RCC typically shows hypervascular enhancement, similar to normal renal cortex. Can be solid or cystic, with irregular enhancement (necrosis/hemorrhage)
- **MRI:** Iso/hypointense on precontrast T1; heterogeneously hyperintense on T2
- **Bosniak classification** used for cystic masses  
  - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)

## Differential Diagnosis

- **Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor**  
  - Low-grade clear cells with tubular/papillary architecture  
  - Nuclei have apical polarization ("piano key"), unlike clear cell RCC  
  - CK7+/CA9+ (basolateral), CD10 and AMACR negative  
  - Indolent, no metastases  
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumorclearcellpapillary.html)
- **Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma (PRCC)**  
  - Papillary, tubular, or solid growth; often foamy macrophages and psammoma bodies  
  - Cytoplasm less clear; nuclei less optically clear than ccRCC  
  - CK7+/AMACR+, CA9 negative, genetic changes (trisomy 7/17, MET mutations)  
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrccpap.html)
- **Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma**  
  - Pale to eosinophilic cells, distinct cell membranes ("plant cell-like"), raisinoid nuclei  
  - CK7 and Hale’s colloidal iron stain diffusely positive, CA9 negative  
    - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrccchromo.html)
- **Oncocytoma**  
  - Mahogany brown tumor, central scar, granular eosinophilic cytoplasm (not clear), round nuclei
  - Negative for CA9, positive for Kit/CD117; lacks classic “chicken-wire” vasculature  
    - [Gu Practical, p.740](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=740)
- **Xp11 Translocation RCC (MiT/TFE3 family)**  
  - Large epithelioid cells, papillary/nested/solid, can have clear cytoplasm; psammoma bodies, TFE3 IHC/fusion, children/young adults
  - TFE3+, negative for VHL mutations  
    - [Gu Practical, p.953](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=953)
- **Metastatic Tumors (e.g., Adrenal, Breast, etc.)**  
  - Non-renal IHC (e.g., inhibin+, ER/PR+, negative for RCC/CA9/PAX8)
  - Context/hx and pattern clues  
    - [Gu Practical, p.977](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=977)
- **Paraganglioma (very rare in kidney)**  
  - Zellballen nests, S100+ sustentacular cells, negative for renal markers (PAX8, CA9), neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin/synaptophysin+)  
    - [Gu Practical, p.964](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=964)
- **Adrenal Rests**  
  - Cortex cells inhibin+, negative for PAX8/RCC; no mass-forming lesion  
    - [Gu Practical, p.683](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=683)

## Prognostic Factors

- AJCC/UICC TNM stage
- WHO/ISUP nuclear grade:
  - Grade 1: inconspicuous/invisible nucleoli @400x
  - Grade 2: nucleoli visible @400x, not @100x
  - Grade 3: prominent nucleoli @100x
  - Grade 4: extreme pleomorphism, multinucleation, sarcomatoid, or rhabdoid change
  - [Pathology Outlines Grading](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantnucleargrading.html)
- Tumor necrosis: strong adverse prognostic factor
- Sarcomatoid or rhabdoid transformation: poor prognosis
- Tumor size, margin status, lymphovascular invasion (LVI—mixed/insufficient evidence)
- Spread to lymph nodes, renal vein/IVC involvement, distant metastases—worse outcomes  
  - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)

## Illustrative Cases

- VHL syndrome: multifocal/bilateral ccRCC with papillary/tubulopapillary pattern but classical immunoprofile  
  - [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantrcc.html)
- Sarcomatoid clear cell RCC: large tumor (>10 cm), mixtures of clear cell and pleomorphic spindle cell morphology  
  - ![Sarcomatoid transformation—gross and microscopic examples](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/_asset_library/textbooks/Gu_Practical/page_images/Gu_Practical_page_0861.png)
- Tumor-to-tumor metastasis: e.g., breast carcinoma metastasizing to a low-grade clear cell RCC; two distinct patterns on morphology and IHC  
  - [Gu Practical, p.977](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/GU_Practical.pdf#page=977)

cards.excerpt: Entity: Collecting duct carcinoma Section: microscopic CDC typically shows tubular and tubulopapillary architectural patterns with irregular, infiltrating glands and associated desmoplastic stroma. Solid nested or sheet-like, trabecular, cord-like individual cells, as well as microcystic patterns, may also be present; a subset show an infiltrative nodular papillary component. The tumour edge is poorly defined, with tumour cells infiltrating between tubules and glomeruli of the adjacent renal parenchyma, which may show dysplasia or atypia within uninvolved tubules. There is often a prominent inflammatory reaction including a neutrophil infiltrate within and around the tumour. Lymphovascular invasion and regional lymph node involvement are common at nephrectomy. cards.entity_name: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney definition: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK) is a rare malignant renal tumour of childhood characterized histologically by variably clear tumour cells and distinctive arborizing fibrovascular septa, and molecularly by BCOR mutations or YWHAE::NUTM2 gene fusion. related_terminology: Not recommended: bone-metastasizing renal tumour of childhood. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: characteristic histomorphology of ovoid tumour cells with nuclear and/or cytoplasmic clearing at least focally, distinctive arborizing fibrovascular septa, and immunoreactivity for cyclin D1 and BCOR. Desirable: features for cases with atypical histomorphology or immunophenotype include molecular identification of BCOR exon 15 ITD or of YWHAE::NUTM2 or BCOR::CCNB3 gene fusion.

cards.title: Clear cell adenocarcinoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell adenocarcinoma definition: Clear cell adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumour consisting of Müllerian-type epithelium with clear cell morphology. related_terminology: None essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: a tumour with clear and hobnail cells in a solid, tubulocystic, confluent, or complex papillary pattern; exclusion of metastasis. Desirable: immunoreactivity for CK7 and PAX8; negativity for mesothelial markers and RCCm.

cards.title: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.entity_name: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour Section: clinical The vast majority of these tumours are incidentally detected. --- The tumour accounts for approximately 3% of cases of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) in adults, with an age range of 8–88 years. The tumours can occur in end-stage renal disease. Tumours of identical morphology that occur in patients with von Hippel–Lindau syndrome appear genomically related to clear cell RCC and distinct from CCPRCT. In 20% and 25% of cases, patients have multifocal and bilateral renal tumours, respectively, and in > 50% of these patients, there is a discordant subtype.

cards.title: Rhabdoid tumour of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Rhabdoid tumour of the kidney Section: ancillary_studies For rhabdoid tumour of the kidney with SMARCA4 inactivation, SMARCA4 (BRG1) immunohistochemistry may be used; this shows a loss of nuclear staining in tumour cells and normal expression in all other cells. Other than by loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) immunostaining, rhabdoid tumour of the kidney and indeed all rhabdoid tumours have a diverse pattern of immunoreactivity, including multiple keratins and vimentin, but also SMA, synaptophysin, and GFAP. Nonspecific polyphenotypic patterns for other antibodies may occur due to trapping of antibodies in hyaline inclusions such as EMA and pancytokeratin. Importantly, over half of rhabdoid tumours show CD99 expression, which may add to the morphological confusion with Ewing sarcoma. Although differential diagnoses are limited in cases with typical morphology and immunohistochemistry, cellular mesoblastic nephroma, plump cell pattern, and clear cell sarcoma of the kidney may be considered. Several renal cell carcinoma morphologies, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma and renal medullary carcinoma, may show rhabdoid morphology with or without SMARCB1 (INI) loss.

cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney Section: diagnostic_molecular_pathology Three characteristic mutations of CCSK are (in decreasing order of frequency) BCOR exon 15 ITD, YWHAE::NUTM2 gene fusion, and BCOR::CCNB3 gene fusion. These three mutations are mutually exclusive.

cards.title: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.entity_name: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour Section: diagnostic_molecular_pathology There are specific molecular pathological features diagnostic of this tumour. Importantly, this tumour lacks chromosome 3p loss and alterations of VHL characteristic of clear cell RCC, and no mutations in TSC1, TSC2, MTOR, or ELOC (TCBE1) (all characteristic of RCC with fibromyomatous or leiomyomatous stroma) have been reported.

cards.title: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney
cards.entity_name: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney Section: ancillary_studies The stromal component is typically positive for actin, desmin, CD10, ER, and PR and frequently the luteinized stromal cells express inhibin and calretinin. Cathepsin K is negative. The epithelial component is PAX2/8-positive. Immunohistochemistry is helpful in the exclusion of renal synovial sarcoma, clear cell papillary tumour, and tubulocystic renal cell carcinoma.

cards.entity_name: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney Section: cytology Cytological diagnosis may be difficult because aspiration specimens may contain occasional groups of cohesive renal epithelial cells, raising the differential diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma.

cards.title: PEComa
cards.excerpt: Entity: PEComa Section: differential_diagnosis In childhood, the diagnosis of PEComa may be extremely challenging because of a relatively large differential diagnosis, which differs depending on the tumour site and can include clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (also known as melanoma of soft parts), alveolar soft part sarcoma, smooth muscle tumours, MiT-family translocation renal cell carcinoma, clear cell sarcoma of the kidney, gastrointestinal stromal tumour, and metastatic melanoma.

Second and third most common RCC subtypes are papillary (10 - 15%) and chromophobe RCC (5%)

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Epidemiology
cards.heading: Epidemiology
cards.text_excerpt:
Incidence: worldwide as of 2020, it is the seventh most common cancer in men (271,249 new cases) and the tenth most common in women (160,039 new cases)
M:F = ~2:1; some subtypes are more common in women (e.g., eosinophilic solid and cystic RCC)
Patients are usually > 50 years old; peak incidence between the ages of 60 and 70 years
~70% of new cases occur in countries with high socioeconomic development
Estimated lifetime prevalence of 2.3% for men and 1.3% for women in the U.S. (JAMA 2024;332:1001)
RCC incidence varies widely from region to region with the highest rates (as of 2018) in Belarus (16.8 cases per 100.000 population), followed by other Central and Eastern European countries
High incidence rates of RCC are also found in the U.S., with an estimated ~81,800 new cases in 2023 and over 14,000 deaths from RCC each year (CA Cancer J Clin 2017;67:7, JAMA 2024;332:1001)

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Hereditary renal cell tumors
cards.heading: Hereditary renal cell tumors
cards.text_excerpt:
Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome
Autosomal dominant, due to germline mutation of VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25
Associated renal lesions: clear cell renal cell carcinoma, benign or atypical renal cysts and numerous microscopic nodules of clear cells (Semin Diagn Pathol 2024;41:20)
RCC in VHL syndrome can be multifocal or bilateral in 50% (eMedicine: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome Imaging [Accessed 7 November 2024])
Clear cell RCC in VHL syndrome may show branching tubulopapillary growth and apical polarization of nuclei resembling clear cell papillary renal cell tumor but shows characteristic molecular and immunohistochemical profile of clear cell RCC
Other associated lesions: hemangioblastomas of cerebellum and retina, pancreatic or liver cysts, clear cell tumors of other sites, papillary cystadenoma of epididymis, pheochromocytoma

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Clinical features
cards.heading: Clinical features
cards.text_excerpt:
Most common manifestation is gross or microscopic hematuria
Classic clinical triad of costovertebral pain, palpable mass and hematuria is present in ~10% of patients
Incidental RCC detection in 37 - 61% of cases due to increased use of imaging; historically, large (10 cm) or already metastatic at diagnosis (JAMA 2024;332:1001)
Great mimicker due to associated paraneoplastic syndromes (20% of patients), including Cushing syndrome, gynecomastia, hypercalcemia, hypertension, leukemoid reaction, polycythemia, Stauffer syndrome (hepatomegaly with hepatic dysfunction), systemic amyloidosis, polyneuromyopathy

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Modality of choice for diagnosis and staging of RCC as well as for posttreatment follow up
cards.heading: Modality of choice for diagnosis and staging of RCC as well as for posttreatment follow up
cards.text_excerpt:
Dedicated renal CT protocols are used
Can differentiate clear cell RCC from non-RCC subtypes with a specificity of up to 100% (Cureus 2021;13:e13231)
RCC may appear solid or cystic, with irregular enhancement due to the presence of necrosis and can show peripheral or central calcifications
Clear cell RCC typically demonstrates hypervascularity and enhancement similar to normal renal cortex as opposed to non-clear cell RCC subtypes (Cureus 2021;13:e13231)
Bosniak classification (5 categories): helps predict risk of malignancy and guides clinical management for cystic renal masses based on contrast enhanced CT imaging (Cureus 2021;13:e13231)

cards.heading: Grade 3: nucleoli prominent at 100x magnification
cards.text_excerpt:

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Staging
cards.heading: Staging
cards.text_excerpt:
Histologic subtype: see Kidney tumor
Necrosis: tumor type necrosis (also known as granular necrosis) has been shown to be an independently significant predictor of a less favorable outcome in clear cell RCC (Pathology 2020;52:507, Histopathology 2019;74:284)
Microscopic coagulative tumor necrosis is also associated with worse outcomes in clear cell and chromophobe RCC (Eur Urol 2021;79:225, Am J Surg Pathol 2013;37:1490)

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Lymphovascular invasion (LVI)
cards.heading: Lymphovascular invasion (LVI)
cards.text_excerpt:

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma overview — Treatment
cards.heading: Treatment
cards.text_excerpt:
Resection (partial or radical nephrectomy) for localized disease
Active surveillance may be an option for comorbid patients with low stage, histologically confirmed low risk tumors
Generally limited use for chemotherapy in RCC management but may be offered to patients with collecting duct or SMARCB1 deficient RCC (formerly medullary carcinoma) (Uroweb: Renal Cell Carcinoma [Accessed 8 November 2024])
Especially in the metastatic setting, it is important to differentiate between clear cell RCC and non-clear cell RCC subtypes, as several HIF1α pathway targeted therapies (e.g., tyrosine kinase inhibitors, anti-VEGF agents) and immune checkpoint inhibitors have been approved for clear cell RCC management in both the U.S. and Europe
HLRCC associated renal tumors frequently require aggressive treatment with specific chemotherapeutic considerations and follow up regimens even if small and solitary (J Natl Compr Canc Netw 2019;17:1278)
Dual immune checkpoint inhibitors combinations (anti-CTLA4 and anti-PDL1) are used in the U.S. as first line treatment for patients with intermediate or poor risk metastatic clear cell RCC (JAMA 2024;332:1001)
